newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda's 1994 genocide set record for speed.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda's 1994 genocide set record for speed.

text.p: The true figure for the number of people killed in Rwanda's genocide in 1994 vanished with corpses stuffed in pit latrines, buried in mass graves or set ablaze.
Estimates range from 500,000 to one million people slaughtered across Rwanda in a three-month orgy of bloodletting, believed to be the fastest genocide of its scale in history.
The main targets were the tiny central Africa country's Tutsi minority but many members of the majority Hutu tribe were also slain as political moderates or opposition supporters.
The slaughter began in early April and ended in June before Tutsi rebels seized power. More than two million Hutus, many of them guilty of the genocide, fled into exile.

The genocide was organised by Hutu hardliners loyal to the late President Juvenal Habyarimana. The butchery was led by soldiers and militiamen but they were helped by countless thousands of ordinary Hutus, either voluntarily or through fear.
French historian Gerard Prunier, working backwards from the number of Tutsis who survived, put the death toll at between 800,000 and 850,000 or more than 10 percent of the population.
He estimated there were 930,000 Tutsis in Rwanda before the slaughter.

The genocide started minutes after the April 6, 1994, killing of Habyarimana when his plane, also carrying Burundi's President Cyprien Ntaryamira, was hit by a rocket and crashed in Kigali. It is not known who killed them.

Presidential guards fanned out in Tutsi neighbourhoods near Kigali airport and started slaughtering men, women and children while other troops killed Tutsi and Hutu moderate leaders, including the prime minister, Agathe Uwilingiyimana, who was also raped.
The killing spread like wildfire across the country. Troops were joined by Hutu militiamen who had been armed months before the genocide. They boasted they could kill 3,000 people an hour.
Local leaders told the Hutu citizenry in public rallies to kill all Tutsis and moderate Hutus. Many of those who refused were accused of cooperating with Tutsi rebels and killed.
Exploiting fears about the approaching Tutsi rebels, troops and militiamen swiftly put up roadblocks in the capital and intercepted fleeing Tutsis or suspected Tutsis and killed them.
The killers were helped by Rwanda's former use of ethnic identity cards.
Tutsis stopped at the checkpoints were slaughtered and their bodies were laid out until convicts in pink uniforms came and picked up the dead, loading them into garbage trucks.
Away from the checkpoints, Hutu soldiers and militiamen roamed neighbourhoods, shooting or hacking to death anyone who ran from them and looting homes and offices.
They searched homes, shops and offices as they went, looking for Tutsis hiding in ceilings and septic tanks.
At Kigali Central Hospital a few days into the genocide, hundreds of corpses were piled into a mound. On top, two dying young men, their throats cuts, cried out for help.
In the southern city of Butare, which was slow to join the frenzy of bloodletting, presidential guards arrived by plane and the local prefect was replaced. Mass killings began in hours.
Terrified Tutsi men, women and children were dragged out of their homes and thrown into large pits lined with tyres doused with petrol and set ablaze.
